claimant_lives_in_uk.description: Whether the claimant lives in the UK.

children.description: A list of children the claimant is claiming for.

lives_with_claimant.description: Whether the child lives with the claimant.

in_approved_education.description: Whether the child is in approved education or training (e.g. A-levels, GCSEs, NVQ up to level 3). Only relevant for children aged 16-19.

in_extension_period.description: Whether the child (aged 16 or 17) has left education and registered with a government-sponsored careers service or the armed forces (qualifying for a 20-week extension).

upkeep_per_week.description: The amount in £ per week the claimant contributes towards the child's upkeep (food, clothes, pocket money, etc.). Only relevant if the child does not live with the claimant.

another_claimant_has_priority.description: Whether another person who also lives with the child has priority for claiming Child Benefit.

another_claimant_lives_with_child.description: Whether someone who lives with the child is already claiming Child Benefit for them.

care_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in local authority care.

care_home_24h_per_week.description: Whether the child spends at least 24 hours per week at home while in local authority care.

hospital_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in hospital or residential accommodation.

claimant_spends_on_child.description: Whether the claimant regularly spends money on the child (e.g. food, clothes, books) while the child is in hospital or residential accommodation.

is_fostered.description: Whether the child is fostered by the claimant.

council_pays_for_child.description: Whether the local council pays towards the child's accommodation or maintenance.

works_24_plus_hours.description: Whether the child works 24 or more hours per week in paid employment.

started_apprenticeship_in_england.description: Whether the child has started an apprenticeship in England.

receives_qualifying_benefits.description: Whether the child receives qualifying benefits in their own right, such as Universal Credit or Employment and Support Allowance.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great! Let me start by understanding your situation. To assess your eligibility for Child Benefit, I need to know about the children you're claiming for.

**First, let me ask about your child/children:**

1. **How many children are you claiming for?**
2. **What are their ages?**

This information will help me determine which path through the eligibility rules is relevant for your situation.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Hi, thanks for helping me with this. I'm looking to claim for my son Alex. He's 17 years old and lives with me at home.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for that context! So you're looking to claim Child Benefit for **Alex, who is 17 years old**.

Since Alex is 17, he falls into the 16-19 age category. For children in this age group, I need to check whether they are in full-time education or approved training.

**Is Alex currently in full-time education or approved training?** (For example, this could be school, college, university, or a formal apprenticeship/training programme)

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, he's not in any education or training at the moment. He finished school and has been working full-time at a local warehouse.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for that information. So Alex is 17, no longer in education or training, and is working full-time.

Let me navigate through the decision tree based on this situation.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Now I need to clarify Alex's situation a bit further. Since Alex is no longer in education or training, I need to check:

**When did Alex finish school/leave education?** Specifically:
- How long ago did he leave (approximately how many weeks ago)?
- This matters because there's a specific timeframe within which young people can still qualify even after leaving education.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: He left school back in June, so that would be... about 6 months ago now. He went straight into the warehouse job after that.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for clarifying. So Alex left school in June, which was approximately 6 months ago (about 26 weeks).

Let me check the specific timeframe for eligibility extension after leaving education.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
I can see that the extension period is 20 weeks. Since Alex left school 6 months ago (approximately 26 weeks), he has passed the 20-week extension window.

This means Alex is no longer eligible for the extension. Let me navigate to the outcome based on this:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Based on the Child Benefit eligibility rules, I have an outcome for you:

## **Result: INELIGIBLE**

**Why Alex doesn't qualify:**

Alex is 17 years old and no longer in approved education or training. While there is a 20-week extension period that allows young people to continue receiving Child Benefit after leaving education (if they register with the careers service or armed forces recruitment), Alex left school 6 months ago (approximately 26 weeks), which is **beyond this 20-week extension window**.

**Key rule:** Child Benefit continues for:
- Children under 16 (automatically)
- Young people aged 16-19 who are in approved education or training
- Young people aged 16-17 who have just left education but within the first 20 weeks (if they register with the careers service or armed forces recruitment)

Since Alex is now working full-time and is outside the 20-week extension period, he is no longer a qualifying child for Child Benefit purposes.

**Next steps:** If your circumstances change (for example, if Alex returns to approved education or training), you may be able to claim again at that point. I'd recommend checking gov.uk or contacting HMRC if you have further questions.
